newsitem.title: USA: 90 million U.S. voters may stay home on Nov. 5.
newsitem.headline: 90 million U.S. voters may stay home on Nov. 5.

text.p: Ninety million Americans who are eligible to vote in Tuesday's U.S. elections may stay home from the polls, a new survey says, echoing other signs around the country pointing to a lukewarm voter turnout.

Thanks to the so-called "Motor Voter" law, which allowed voters to register when they renewed their drivers' licences or performed other chores, the actual percentage of registered voters has risen three percentage points to 67.7 percent since 1992, putting 5 million more people on the voter rolls.

But just because more voters register does not mean they will cast ballots, said Curtis Gans, director of the Committee for the Study of the American Electorate, which conducted the survey of voter turnout.

"The most likely scenario is that despite the Motor Voter law ... increases in registration, voter turnout will drop sharply this year ... from the 55.2 percent who voted in 1992," Gans said. However, it will likely be greater than the recent low turnout of 1988, when only 50.1 percent voted.
Except for 1992, when concern over a weak economy spurred voters to the polls, this year's expected decline is part of a 35-year trend toward ever-lower voter turnout, according to the survey.
"Recessions and anger can cause one-election increases in turnout," Gans said. "Sustained participation depends on the opposite -- hope."

"Because of a variety of things -- the way we conduct our campaigns, the alignment of our political parties, the cynicism of the press and public, and the lack of civil values, among many other things -- there is precious little of that hope around today."

The survey also found an overall decline in interest and intent to vote on Tuesday, a one-third decrease in the number of people who watched televised presidential and vice presidential debates, and a 40 percent drop in the amount of nightly news time devoted to politics, which the survey said was a commercial decision based on lack of viewer interest.

The United States has one of the lowest voter turnout rates among industrialised nations, according to the League of Women Voters, which found that only 53 percent of U.S. registered voters went to the polls on average in the 1980s, compared with 94 percent in top-ranked Belgium.
Only Switzerland, among industrialised nations, had a lower turnout rate, with 49 percent.
Low voter turnout accentuates the gap between rich and poor, according to Fordham University political scientist Tom DeLuca: When fewer voters vote, fewer poor people are represented.

In years like this one, DeLuca said in a statement, far higher percentages of well-educated, well-employed, economically comfortable people will vote, compared with the poorly educated, indigent and under-employed.

Outside the ballot box, the better-off tend to be more closely engaged in public life than poor people, DeLuca said, from attending public meetings to writing letters to members of Congress to contributing money for a political candidate.

"Voting turnout is so depressed in the United States and the class voting gap so wide, because of biases built into the heart of our political system," DeLuca said. "Nothing short of serious structural reform can remedy these defects."

A University of Iowa study seconded Gans's predictions of low voter turnout, and said that would benefit Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole and Republican candidates for the House of Representatives. A higher turnout would hurt Dole and help Reform Party candidate Ross Perot but would not help President Bill Clinton very much, the study found.

"The expected lower turnout relative to 1992 is the result of a drop in interest inthe campaign and a continued growth in the feeling that politicians just don't care about the average person," the Iowa study said.
